newsitem.title: AUSTRIA: Austria top banks deny they acted as cartel.
newsitem.headline: Austria top banks deny they acted as cartel.

text.p: Two of Austria's top banks denied allegations on Wednesday that they were involved in a cartel to set interest rates and fees to clients in breach of European Union law.

Far-right leader Joerg Haider charged that the nation's banking system was riddled with corruption and claimed he could back up his accusations with documents sent to opposition parties and state prosecutors by a senior financier before he committed suicide.

The head of the populist Freedom Party claimed he had copies of official papers supporting allegations that leading banks had acted as a cartel in setting borrowing and lending rates, charges to customers and fixing advertising strategy.
"This is the way the mafia operates. In Italy the mafia is a private organisation, in Austria it is state-owned," Haider told a news conference.
The country's two leading banks swiftly issued statements rejecting the allegations. Bank Austria denied there had been any illegal inter-bank agreements.
Creditanstalt said cartel deals would be senseless in what it termed a competitive banking sector.
"We do not know anything about these documents," a Creditanstalt spokesman told Reuters.

First allegations of a scandal involving Austria's political and financial establishment surfaced at the end of April following the suicide of Gerhard Praschak, board member of Kontrollbank (OeKB), the central securities depository and government financing agent.
Before he died, Praschak sent a 120-page document to all opposition parties and state prosecutors.
Haider based his accusation of interest rate fixing on papers purportedly written by Praschak.
The document, copies of which were made available to reporters, lists lending and borrowing conditions for private as well as corporate customers.
"From the papers it is clear that the banks, together with the central bank, set their business conditions behind closed doors," Haider alleged.
"Such agreements contravene Austria's cartel laws, are against banking principles and European Union fair trade laws. We will draw this matter to the attention of the European Commission," he added.
There was no immediate comment from the Oesterreichische Nationalbank, the Austrian central bank.

Parliament, dominated by the ruling Social Democrats and the conservative People's Party, on Tuesday voted down a call by all three opposition parties, including the Greens and liberals, for an inquiry into the Praschak affair.
Haider renewed his call for a parliamentary inquiry into the Kontrollbank, which is jointly owned by leading commercial banks, including Bank Austria and Creditanstalt.

Last week Haider produced documents purportedly provided by Praschak which alleged that Bank Austria and Creditanstalt had prompted the Kontrollbank board in 1994 secretly to award its shareholders a special payment totalling 140 million schillings ($12 million) on which no tax was paid.

Bank Austria and Creditanstalt denied the allegations. Austrian tax authorities announced on Tuesday they had launched an inquiry into the Kontrollbank. No one at Kontrollbank was available for comment.
